title: Check yourself: where a Predicate is passed

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A method prunes cancelled bookings with `bookings.removeIf(Booking::cancelled)`. Its unit test passes `Arrays.asList(...)` holding three active bookings, and the call returns `false`. In production the caller passes `List.copyOf(...)` of three active bookings. What does the call do there?

options.text: It returns false as in the test, since removeIf changes a list only when an element matches, and none does
options.says: whether removeIf may run is up to the list; an unmodifiable list throws before testing anything

options.text: It returns false as in the test, since both kinds of list refuse only calls that add elements, and none is made
options.says: the removeIf of List.copyOf throws before testing any element, so it refuses removal, not only additions

options.text: It throws UnsupportedOperationException, since that list refuses removeIf before testing any element
options.says: an unmodifiable List refuses every mutator; its removeIf throws even when no element would be removed

options.text: It throws UnsupportedOperationException, since that list refuses removeIf after testing every element
options.says: it throws before testing any element; the predicate is never called

origin.section: removeIf Is the Safe Way to Remove While Iterating, and an Immutable List Refuses It Even When Nothing Matches

questions.stem: `for (Ticket t : open) if (t.isSpam()) open.remove(t);` runs over an `ArrayList` of five tickets, of which the fourth and the fifth are spam. What is the outcome?

options.text: The list ends with three tickets, since the loop removes the fourth and then tests and removes the fifth
options.says: after the fourth is removed, hasNext() compares position 4 with size 4 and the loop ends; the fifth is never tested

options.text: The list ends with four tickets, since the loop stops after removing the fourth and never tests the fifth
options.says: removing the fourth shrinks the list to four, hasNext() returns false at position 4, and no next() call gets to throw

options.text: The loop throws ConcurrentModificationException, since removing the fourth makes the loop's next step fail
options.says: the check runs in next(); removing the fourth makes hasNext() false, so next() is never called and nothing throws

options.text: The loop throws ConcurrentModificationException, since the loop moves on to the fifth after the list has changed
options.says: the loop never reaches the fifth ticket: hasNext() is false once the list has shrunk to the loop's position

origin.section: removeIf Is the Safe Way to Remove While Iterating, and an Immutable List Refuses It Even When Nothing Matches

questions.stem: Payments are listed in time order. A team writes a `distinctBy(Payment::cardId)` predicate backed by `ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet()` and runs `payments.parallelStream().filter(distinctBy(Payment::cardId)).toList()` to get each card's first payment. What does the list hold?

options.text: Each card's first payment, since the thread-safe set records every card once and loses no update
options.says: the set is right, but which payment reaches it first depends on the threads, not on time order

options.text: Each card's first payment, since filter on an ordered parallel stream tests the payments in list order
options.says: filter keeps the passing elements in encounter order but promises nothing about the order in which it tests them

options.text: One payment for each card, the one some worker thread tested first, since threads test payments in no fixed order
options.says: whichever thread reaches a card first wins; in the runs on the page that was never the first element

options.text: Two payments for some cards, the ones two worker threads tested at once, since the set is shared between the threads
options.says: a thread-safe set stops the lost updates; the runs on the page kept exactly one order per customer

origin.section: A Predicate That Remembers Answers Differently in Parallel and on Its Second Use

questions.stem: A coupon form validates with `Pattern.compile("^[A-Z]{4}-\\d{2}$").asPredicate()`. A colleague proposes `Pattern.compile("[A-Z]{4}-\\d{2}").asMatchPredicate()` instead. Which input does the current validator accept and the proposed one reject?

options.text: "SALE-25\n", since $ also matches just before a line break at the very end of the input
options.says: by default $ matches before a final line terminator, so find() succeeds; matches() needs the whole input

options.text: "SALE-25\n\n", since $ also matches just before a run of line breaks at the very end of the input
options.says: $ makes an exception for one final line terminator only; with two, find() fails

options.text: "xSALE-25", since find() may start its match after the first character even when the pattern begins with ^
options.says: ^ ties the match to the start of the input, so find() fails on a leading character

options.text: "SALE-25x", since find() may end its match before the last character even when the pattern ends with $
options.says: $ ties the match to the end of the input, apart from a final line terminator, so a trailing letter fails

origin.section: asPredicate Finds the Pattern Anywhere; asMatchPredicate Needs the Whole String

concepts: Removing inside a for-each throws ConcurrentModificationException at the next next(), except when the removal makes hasNext() false, and then the last element is silently never tested.
An unmodifiable list such as List.of or List.copyOf throws UnsupportedOperationException from removeIf even when no element matches; Arrays.asList throws only when one does.
In a parallel stream a stateful predicate's answer depends on the order threads test elements, so even a thread-safe seen-set keeps an arbitrary element per key; a collector keeps the first.
